pharm: Synthetic decapeptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist that, after an initial stimulatory phase, produces pituitary desensitization and reversible medical castration (suppression of LH, FSH, testosterone and estradiol).
quick: Prostate Ca: 500 mcg SC q8h x7d then 200 mcg SC daily, or 1.2 mg/day intranasal
Testosterone/estradiol, PSA, bone density, symptoms of flare
summary: Buserelin is a GnRH (LHRH) agonist used for advanced hormone-dependent prostate cancer, endometriosis, and as part of controlled ovarian stimulation in assisted reproduction. Continuous administration first transiently stimulates then down-regulates pituitary GnRH receptors, suppressing sex-hormone production to castrate/postmenopausal levels. It is marketed in Europe and elsewhere (e.g., Suprefact, Suprecur) but is not FDA-approved in the United States. An initial testosterone/estrogen surge can cause a transient tumor flare in prostate cancer, so anti-androgen cover is recommended at initiation.
indications: Advanced hormone-dependent prostate carcinoma (palliative endocrine treatment)
Endometriosis (where surgery is not immediately indicated)
Pituitary down-regulation prior to and during controlled ovarian stimulation in assisted reproduction (IVF)
Other hormone-responsive conditions per local SmPC (e.g., uterine fibroids in some regions)

dosage.t: Every 8 hours (1.5 mg/day) for the first 7 days
dosage.n: Per Suprefact SmPC; give with an anti-androgen to cover the testosterone flare
Continue after the initial 7-day SC induction

dosage.d: 400 mcg (1 spray of 100 mcg into each nostril, 2 sprays per dose)
dosage.n: Begun after the initial 7-day SC course; long-term maintenance

dosage.d: 150 mcg (1 spray of 150 mcg) in each nostril
dosage.n: Start on days 1-2 of the menstrual cycle; usual duration up to 6 months, do not repeat course

dosage.d: SC 200-500 mcg/day; or intranasal 150 mcg per nostril up to ~4 times daily
dosage.t: Daily until down-regulation, then continued with gonadotropin stimulation
dosage.n: Follow the specific assisted-reproduction protocol and SmPC; dose/route vary by regimen

admin: Subcutaneous injection: rotate sites (abdomen); the first SC induction phase typically lasts 7 days
Intranasal: clear the nose before use; one metered spray per nostril per the indication-specific dose; avoid nasal decongestants around dosing as they may reduce absorption
For prostate cancer, start an anti-androgen a few days before and continue for about 2-3 weeks to prevent disease flare from the initial testosterone surge
For endometriosis and IVF, timing relative to the menstrual cycle is important - follow the protocol
Do not interrupt therapy without medical advice; in prostate cancer interruption allows testosterone recovery
moa: Buserelin is a potent GnRH receptor agonist. Initial dosing stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH (causing a transient rise in testosterone or estradiol - the flare). With continuous administration, GnRH receptors are down-regulated and the pituitary becomes desensitized, suppressing gonadotropin and consequently gonadal sex-hormone secretion to castrate (men) or postmenopausal (women) levels, depriving hormone-dependent tissues of their stimulus.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to buserelin, other GnRH analogs, or excipients
Hormone-independent prostate cancer or prior orchidectomy (no benefit)
relative: Risk of tumor flare in prostate cancer (cover with anti-androgen)
Pre-existing metabolic bone disease / osteoporosis risk (long-term use)
Ureteric obstruction or spinal cord metastases in prostate cancer (flare may worsen)
monitor: Bone mineral density with prolonged use
Symptoms of disease flare in the first weeks

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy; exclude pregnancy before starting in women. Use non-hormonal contraception during treatment for benign gynecological indications.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established in the SmPC; the peptide is metabolized rather than dependent on renal excretion of unchanged drug.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established; use with general caution.

major: Drugs that prolong the QT interval - additive risk as androgen-deprivation therapy can prolong QT (consider in prostate cancer)
moderate: Antidiabetic agents (insulin, oral hypoglycemics) - androgen/estrogen deprivation may alter glucose tolerance and dosing needs
Other hormonal therapies - may counteract or alter effect
minor: Nasal decongestants - may reduce absorption of the intranasal formulation if used close to dosing
interactions.diagnostics: Suppresses gonadotropin (LH/FSH) and sex-steroid levels; interferes with pituitary-gonadal function tests during therapy.

common: Loss of libido, vaginal dryness, amenorrhea (women)
Injection-site reactions; nasal irritation with the spray
serious: Tumor flare in prostate cancer (worsening bone pain, urinary obstruction, spinal cord compression)
Reduced bone mineral density / osteoporosis with prolonged use
Cardiovascular events / QT prolongation (with androgen deprivation)
rare: Pituitary apoplexy (in patients with pituitary adenoma)
Ovarian hyperstimulation when used in assisted reproduction
emergency: Spinal cord compression from prostate cancer flare

monitoring: Serum testosterone (prostate cancer) or estradiol (gynecological use)
PSA and clinical response in prostate cancer
Symptoms of tumor flare during the first 1-2 weeks
Bone mineral density with long-term therapy
counsel: Symptoms (and prostate cancer signs) may briefly worsen in the first week or two before improving - an anti-androgen is given to cover this
Hot flushes, reduced libido, and sexual dysfunction are expected effects of lowering hormone levels
Use the nasal spray correctly and consistently; do not use decongestant sprays around the same time
Long-term use can weaken bones - your clinician may monitor bone density and advise calcium/vitamin D or exercise
Women: use non-hormonal contraception and report any pregnancy; periods usually stop during treatment and return afterwards
pk: Initial gonadotropin/testosterone rise within hours to days; suppression over ~1-3 weeks
SC plasma peak ~1-2 h; intranasal lower bioavailability (~1-3%)
Castrate hormone levels maintained with continued daily dosing
Store per SmPC (typically below 25 C; do not freeze); protect injection from light
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the United States; marketed in Europe and other regions as Suprefact / Suprecur (source: EMA-region SmPC / product information)
Continuous agonist exposure paradoxically suppresses the pituitary - the basis of GnRH-agonist 'medical castration'
Always anticipate the initial testosterone/estrogen flare; in prostate cancer give anti-androgen cover (start before and continue ~2-3 weeks) to prevent disease flare
Long-term androgen/estrogen deprivation reduces bone density - monitor and consider bone-protective measures
Intranasal route is convenient but has low, variable bioavailability and depends on correct technique and intact nasal mucosa
missed: Maintain regular dosing for reliable suppression. SC: give the missed dose as soon as remembered. Intranasal: take the missed spray when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose; do not double up. Prolonged gaps allow hormone levels to recover - contact the clinician if doses are missed repeatedly.
overdose: No specific antidote; experience is limited. Effects are extensions of pharmacology (profound hormone suppression). Discontinue and provide supportive, symptomatic care with monitoring of hormone levels until recovery.
